This book uses four **Canonical Cluster Tiers**\index{Assumptions!cluster tiers} (256, 2,048, 8,192, and 100,000 GPUs) to illustrate how system behavior changes across scale. They are editorial reference points aligned with common research-lab, production, large-training, and hyperscale fleets, not measurements from a single deployment. @Tbl-fleet-cluster-sizes defines GPU counts; chapters derive node counts, failure rates, and network requirements from these baselines and the assumptions in subsequent tables.

Distributed training and inference are bottlenecked by data movement between machines as often as by computation within them. **Network Assumptions**\index{Assumptions!network} fix bandwidth and latency for every interconnect tier, from NVLink/PCIe within a node [@nvidia2017gpu; @NVIDIA2020; @choquette2023], through InfiniBand, RDMA, and Ethernet fabrics [@infiniband2000spec; @gangidi2024rdma; @nvidia2026quantumX800; @ethernetAlliance2025roadmap], to the speed-of-light WAN floor (physics identity).

At fleet scale, component failures are not exceptional events but statistical certainties. **Reliability Assumptions**\index{Assumptions!reliability} here fix Mean Time To Failure (MTTF) for each major component class in a data-center GPU node and the time to detect and recover from failures. These values drive analysis in @sec-fault-tolerance-reliability and scheduling in @sec-fleet-orchestration; deeper failure modeling appears in @sec-appdx-reliability-foundations.

The environmental impact of fleet-scale ML depends on three factors: how much power the facility draws beyond the IT equipment (PUE), how much water the cooling system consumes (WUE), and how much carbon the local grid emits per kilowatt-hour. **Sustainability Assumptions**\index{Assumptions!sustainability} here support @sec-sustainable-ai and total-cost-of-ownership estimates in @sec-ops-scale.

**Capacity-Planning Assumptions**\index{Assumptions!capacity planning} quantify two related phenomena: (1) the fraction of peak hardware performance that real workloads achieve (Model FLOPs Utilization), and (2) how efficiently that performance scales as more machines are added (scaling efficiency). Together they determine the effective compute available for a given cluster size and budget—the number that matters for project planning.
